analysis.one_liner: Bans charging women more than men for substantially similar products and services.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 13, 2025 with 27 cosponsors, the Pink Tax Repeal Act has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no action since referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to charge different prices for products or services that are substantially the same but marketed to different genders — the pattern often called the 'pink tax,' where women's razors, shampoos, or dry cleaning cost more than the men's equivalent. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of residents to win refunds and stop the practice. The bill has not moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Women consumers, who studies have long shown pay more for functionally identical products marketed in pink packaging or labeled for women. All consumers gain a clearer rule that identical goods must carry identical prices regardless of gendered marketing. State attorneys general also gain a new tool to win restitution for residents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women buying everyday goods and services

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits selling two substantially similar consumer products from the same manufacturer at different prices based on the gender they are marketed to, and bars the same for substantially similar services [S2].

Defines 'substantially similar' so that differences in color, materials, intended use, and functional design decide the question for products, and time, difficulty, and cost of providing decide it for services — so real cost differences are allowed but color alone is not [S2].

Lets the FTC treat violations as unfair or deceptive practices with its full enforcement powers, and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents to enjoin violations and obtain damages or restitution [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of consumer products (personal care, razors, clothing) and service providers (dry cleaning, hair care, alterations) who currently price women's versions higher would lose that pricing margin, bear compliance costs, and face FTC penalties and state lawsuits if they do not equalize prices. Some of that cost could show up as slightly higher prices on the men's versions rather than lower prices on women's.
analysis.who_pays_short: Personal care makers and service providers

drawbacks.text: The 'substantially similar' standard invites argument: manufacturers could make small changes to materials or features to claim products are not similar, keeping differential pricing in place [S2].
The ban is a price mandate on private sellers; if companies respond by raising the men's version rather than cutting the women's, consumers could pay the same overall and the bill's benefit shrinks.

Service prices can legitimately reflect differences in time, skill, and cost; the bill tries to handle this by defining similar services by those factors, but drawing the line case by case could mean litigation and enforcement uncertainty for small businesses [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but modest per household: eliminating the gap where women pay more for nearly identical goods. The main weaknesses are enforcement — companies can game the similarity test — and the possibility that prices equalize upward rather than downward. On balance it is a targeted consumer protection with manageable costs, but its value depends on how aggressively the FTC and state attorneys general actually use it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on May 13, 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Norma Torres introduced the Pink Tax Repeal Act in the House on May 13, 2025 [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history [S4].
27 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears in the cosponsor list [S3].
The bill text would bar gender-based price differences on substantially similar products and services, with FTC enforcement and state attorney general lawsuits to win restitution for residents [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and service providers that price women's versions of products higher are better off for now, since the bill has not advanced and the practice remains legal under federal law.

for.name: Rep. Norma Torres
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

against.name: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee chair controlling the markup calendar
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 13, 2025 and has taken no further action — no hearing or markup has been scheduled [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors are House Democrats and none are Republicans, and the bill sits in a Republican-controlled committee that has not acted on it [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Consumer products manufacturers (personal care, razors, apparel)
industries.note: These companies profit from selling women's versions of substantially similar products at higher prices; the bill would force them to equalize prices or risk FTC penalties and state restitution suits. Its gain is ordinary consumers' cost.

industries.industry: Personal service providers (dry cleaning, salons, alterations)
industries.note: Service businesses that charge women more for similar work would have to justify pricing by time, difficulty, or cost or equalize prices. Some real cost differences are protected, but gendered pricing alone would be illegal.

analysis.trajectory: With no hearing or markup after referral and no Republican support in a Republican-controlled committee, the bill is unlikely to advance this Congress. Prior versions of the Pink Tax Repeal Act in earlier Congresses also died in committee without a floor vote.
